title: Shakti as a philosophy
hook: sages ask what caused the world, then sit down to meditate, and see a power hidden in plain sight

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kena Upanishad: fire couldn't burn a blade of grass, wind couldn't lift it, and Uma named the power behind them, Brahman.

What is the cause? Where did we come from? By what do we live? Where do we rest? Those are the questions that open the Shvetashvatara Upanishad. A group of seekers run through the usual answers: time, nature, chance, the elements. None of them settles it. So they turn from the list. They sit, and they meditate. And the next verse says what they saw. Not a new theory. A power, hidden. Today the word shakti steps out of the stories and into an Upanishad.
screen: `WHAT IS THE CAUSE?` → `THE USUAL ANSWERS DON'T SETTLE IT.` → `THEY STOP TALKING, AND SIT.`

segments.voice: Here is the verse, in paraphrase. Those who followed the path of meditation saw the power of God's own self, hidden in its own qualities. The Sanskrit is devatma shakti: the shakti of the divine self. Notice three things. First, it's seen in meditation, not argued into. The list ran out, they sat, and then they saw. Second, the power is hidden in a surprising place: in its own qualities. The power behind the world is covered by the world it makes, the way a person can be hidden by their own good work. You see the painting and forget the painter's hand. Third, the power belongs to God's own self. It isn't a second thing standing beside God. Later the same Upanishad comes back to it. His highest power, the text says, is heard of as many-sided, and his knowledge, strength and action belong to his nature. Knowing, strength, doing: shakti is the name for God in action. One more line draws the map. Know that maya is prakriti, nature, and that the great Lord is the one who wields maya. Teachers read the word maya there in more than one way, but the shape of the verse is plain: the power that makes nature is in the Lord's hand. In this Upanishad, the power that makes and moves the world isn't outside the divine. It's God's own, folded so deeply into what we see that it takes stillness to notice it.
screen: `THE SEEKERS SIT AND MEDITATE.` · `GOD'S OWN POWER, HIDDEN IN ITS QUALITIES.` · `KNOWING, STRENGTH, DOING.` · `THE LORD WIELDS MAYA.` · then, large: `DEVATMA SHAKTI.`

segments.voice: Let one big question come to mind, your own version of where did this come from, and don't answer it. When a thought comes with an answer, let it pass like the seekers' list, and keep looking, the way you'd wait for an animal to step out of the trees. If you pray, you can rest in the name you use for God; if you don't, rest in the looking.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the Shvetashvatara Upanishad, seekers in meditation see God's own power, hidden in its own qualities.
Your line: Shakti as a philosophy. You see the painting, and the painter's hand is hidden in it. That's day one thousand eighty-four.

howItsDone: The Shvetashvatara Upanishad is read and chanted in Vedanta and Shaiva study, and its verse on God's hidden power is quoted by teachers explaining the idea of shakti.

chat.says: What did the seekers in the Shvetashvatara find when their list of causes ran out?
options: They sat in meditation and saw God's own power, hidden in its own qualities.
A sage walked in and handed them the answer, written out on a palm leaf.
They found a second god, standing apart from the first, who made the world.
chat.meaning: In meditation they saw devatma shakti, the power of God's own self, hidden in its own qualities: not a second thing beside God.

notes: 1.1–1.2 paraphrased: the opening questions (kiṃ kāraṇaṃ brahma, kutaḥ sma jātāḥ, jīvāmaḥ kena, kva ca sampratiṣṭhāḥ) and the candidate causes (kāla, svabhāva, niyati, yadṛcchā, bhūtāni). The hook lists 'time, nature, chance, the elements'; confirm 'nature' for svabhāva and 'chance' collapsing niyati/yadṛcchā.
1.3 devātmaśaktiṃ svaguṇair nigūḍhām: 'hidden in its own qualities' vs. 'hidden by its own gunas'; Keeper to choose.
4.10 māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ vidyān māyinaṃ tu maheśvaram: the two readings of maya (illusion / creative power) are named without ranking.
The painter image is the writer's illustration, not the text's.
